summary: Suggests a mail protocol mapping between full RFC 822 messages and RFC 822 with restricted encoding, for the Internet and UK Academic communities. It asks for discussion and is not a standard. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Some mail systems can only handle simple text. This describes how to turn fancy mail into simple mail and back.

questions: mapping between rfc 822 and restricted encoding
how to encode rfc 822 addresses for uucp
what does #h# mean in an email address
subtitle: A reversible encoding that lets awkward RFC 822 addresses survive mail systems with a restricted character set.

tldr.problem: Some mail networks, such as those using UUCP transfer, cannot carry the full RFC 822 character set in addresses, so messages with quoted-string local parts may be lost.
tldr.mechanism: A symmetric mapping rewrites the local part: spaces become underscore and other awkward characters become short codes such as #h# or three-digit decimal codes between hashes.
tldr.outcome: It was a memo seeking discussion, not an Internet standard, and it is now Historic.

today: RFC 1137 is Historic and it updates RFC 976. Its own text says it is not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Full and Restricted RFC 822
sections.content:
Some mail networks that use RFC 822 cannot support its full character set. The memo defines two terms. Full RFC 822 supports any legal address, including the quoted-string form of local part such as "Joe Soap"@foo.bar. Restricted RFC 822 need not support the quoted-string form; standard UUCP mail transfer is an example.

Moving a message from full to restricted can lose it, for instance when no error message can be returned. The memo describes a quoting mechanism to avoid that. It derives from a mapping in RFC 987.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail pipes only accept plain letters. This note explains how to disguise fancy addresses so they fit through.

sections.title: The Encoding
sections.content:
The memo defines an atom-encoded form in the RFC 822 EBNF notation. Ordinary characters pass through unchanged. A space becomes _. Other special characters get codes: #u# for an underscore, #l# and #r# for parentheses, #m# for a comma, #c# for a colon, #b# for a backslash, #h# for a hash, #e# for an equals sign and #s# for a slash. Any other character can be written as #nnn#, where the three digits are its ASCII value in decimal (0 to 127).

To encode, first remove any quoting from the quoted-string, then pass the allowed characters directly and encode the rest. To decode, reverse the mapping if the address parses as an encoded atom, and otherwise map the characters directly.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a secret code: a space becomes an underscore, and other tricky symbols become little tags like #h#. You can always turn it back.

sections.title: Where It Applies and Examples
sections.content:
The mapping should be used for all addresses, at the MTS or header level, and is applied to the local part. The RFC's table shows that Steve.Kille@cs.ucl.ac.uk is unchanged, "Steve Kille"@cs.ucl.ac.uk becomes Steve_Kille@cs.ucl.ac.uk, and "argle#~"@blargle becomes argle#h##126#@blargle.

The memo says security issues are not discussed in it.
sections.plainLanguage: A name with a space gets an underscore instead. A name with a strange symbol gets a number code. A plain name stays the same.
